items: Keep the thing You joined from being pulled apart
Show me whose hands are holding us

verse.text: So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.

blocks.text: Jesus states the arithmetic clearly: no longer two, but one. That single sentence is the most countercultural thing in Scripture about marriage — the world counts couples as two individuals who negotiate; heaven counts them as one flesh who cooperate. Every decision, every budget, every parenting call, every plan for the future runs through the union before it runs through individual preference. 'No longer two' is not the loss of yourselves; it is the gaining of a whole.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Check one decision today through the 'one flesh' lens
Ask: 'is this what's best for us, not just me?'
Celebrate that you're a whole, not two halves

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach us to decide as one, not negotiate as two
Make the union the first question, not the last

verse.text: 'For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.' This is a profound mystery—but I am talking about Christ and the church.

blocks.text: Paul takes the same Genesis sentence and announces it points beyond itself: marriage is a picture of Christ and the church. That vaults your ordinary Tuesday — the dishes, the argument, the goodnight — into something cosmic. Every act of love in your marriage is a small sermon about Christ's love. Every forgiveness is a rehearsal of the gospel. You are not merely maintaining a household; you are displaying, to a watching world and to your children, the shape of grace.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name one way your marriage pictures Christ and the church
Do one small loving act that 'tells the gospel'
See your spouse as the one God gave to show you His love

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make us a true picture of Christ and the church
Let our love preach without words

verse.text: They become one flesh.

blocks.text: Quiz day on oneness. One truth to hold above every storm: the union is God's work, so it rests on His holding, not your grip. Check what you remember, then act like you believe it.

blocks.question: In Genesis 2:24, marriage becomes one flesh through what?
options: Years of compatibility
God's joining of a man and a wife
Negotiating and compromise
Shared goals
blocks.explain: 'A man... is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.' The union is made, not manufactured.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep me believing in the oneness You made
Let today run through the union

verse.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the rest begins with an economist's line: two are better than one, because their labor has a good return. Marriage is the arrangement God designed for the work of life to actually pay. Parenting pays more held together. Building, working, serving, enduring — all of it 'returns' better in twos. Let that settle: you are not carrying the same load in a smaller boat. You are two hands on one oar. Rest in the math.

blocks.prompt: Where has being two shown you a 'good return' your single self could never have produced? Rest in that today.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Thank You for the good return of being two
Let me rest in our two-ness, not carry as one

verse.text: Though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken.

blocks.text: The week ends at the most famous verse about the twoness of marriage — three strands. The third strand is God. A marriage covenant has three parties: you, your spouse, and the One who joined you. When the two of you are pressed, the third strand is what keeps the cord from snapping. Week one closes with the cord already braided: husband, wife, and the Lord holding all three of you together.

blocks.prompt: Describe a time the 'third strand' held your marriage when the two of you were overpowered. What does that memory change about how you face the next storm?
blocks.placeholder: The time the third strand held us was...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be the third strand that is never broken
Hold the three of us together under the press

intro.text: The house you're building is framed in what you say to each other. The same mouth that can level a wall in a sentence can raise one in another. This week we take the words seriously, because the marriage depends on them.

verse.text: The tongue has the power of life and death, and those who love it will eat its fruit.

blocks.text: Death and life — that is the stakes the proverb puts on ordinary conversation. The tongue doesn't merely reflect a marriage; it grows it or corrodes it. 'I'm proud of you' and 'what's wrong with you?' — both are seeds. The fruit of what you say to each other gets eaten: by the marriage, by the children who learn your tone, by the room you live in. Before you build cabinets and savings, watch the building material audited at your table: the words.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Catch your tone mid-sentence at least once today
Say one life-word you've been withholding
Ask: 'does what I'm about to say build or bury?'

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Tune my tongue to life, not death
Let the fruit of our words feed our house

verse.text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

blocks.text: Wrath is coming — the heat of a disagreement is going to arrive sometime. The proverb says what you do with it depends on the answer: a gentle answer turns it away; a harsh word stirs it. The gentle answer is not the weak answer; it is the powerful one that ends fights nobody wins. When your spouse comes hot, your first word can be the wall that makes it worse or the hand that turns the storm. Practice the gentle answer — it works down the staff, too.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Rehearse gentleness before the next hard talk
Choose a gentle opening when the heat comes
Notice what 'gentle' does to the anger in your house

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give me the gentle answer when it counts
Turn our wrath away before it turns on us

verse.text: Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will grow to become in every respect the mature body of him who is the head, that is, Christ.

blocks.text: Two mistakes destroy marriages in one-choice increments: truth without love (harsh, 'just being honest') and love without truth (silent, 'I didn't want to hurt them'). Paul's 'instead' is the third way: speak the truth IN love. The truth is the content; love is the manner. Both matter, and both take practice. A marriage that tells each other the truth gently grows up; a marriage that does either one alone begins to calcify.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Say one truth you've been dodging — lovingly
Ask forgiveness for a truth said without love
Receive a truth your spouse gentles you with

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let our truth-telling carry our love
Grow us up by the way we speak

verse.text: Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building others up according to their needs, that it may benefit those who listen.

blocks.text: The verse's audit is a hard one: not just 'no unwholesome talk' but 'only what is helpful for building others up according to their needs.' Not your convenience, not your venting — their needs. Your husband needs encouragement today, not critique; your wife needs a listening ear, not a fix. The question that passes words through this gate: is this building them up? If it isn't, it doesn't get said. That gate, installed on both mouths, rebuilds a whole marriage.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Ask your spouse: 'what do you need from words today?'
Say one building-up thing matched to their need
Gate your criticism for one full day

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let my mouth be a builder of my spouse
Show me their need before their faults

verse.text: The tongue has the power of life and death.

blocks.text: Quiz day on words. One discipline to own: every sentence is a seed, so watch what your mouth plants. Check what you remember, then go water something good.

blocks.question: According to Proverbs 18:21, what does the tongue have power to do?
options: Only to entertain
To wound or heal deeply
To give life and death
To influence the weather
blocks.explain: 'The tongue has the power of life and death.' Proverbs 18:21 — the stakes of your words are literally life and death.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Guard what my tongue is planting
Let our kitchen be a greenhouse of life-words

verse.text: Her children arise and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her.

blocks.text: Rest day — and rest begins with praise. The famous chapter about the capable wife ends not with her performance but with her husband's praise. She is spoken well of in her own home; her husband's first mouth-work is celebration, not correction. Whatever the divi of the two of you — the saver, the planner, the doer — the rest posture is praise. Say something good about your spouse today, in the hearing of your own heart, with nothing else attached. That is rest for both of you.

blocks.prompt: When did you last praise your spouse — not flattery, not 'nice job on chores', but real public-hearted praise? Plan your one honest line of praise today.
blocks.placeholder: The praise I need to give is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make me a praising spouse
Let my words anoint, not audit, my husband/wife

verse.text: Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.

blocks.text: The week closes on the word that should be the wallpaper of your house: encourage. Build each other up. Not 'be encouraging when things go well' — the verse assumes it as your practice: 'just as in fact you are doing.' Encouragement is the counter-weight to the world's daily discouragement; your spouse gets enough from outside, and the one place they should never get it is from you. Week two turns the house to face this fixed point: our words build or they don't come out.

blocks.prompt: What would change in your week if every sentence you spoke to your spouse had to pass the build-up test first? Where do you need to fortify the gate?
blocks.placeholder: The one gate I need installed is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make our house famous for encouragement
Build us both up through each other's mouths

intro.text: Every marriage fights. The health of a marriage is not the absence of conflict — it is how the conflict is fought. This week is not about ending arguments but about fighting them the way that doesn't hurt the thing you're fighting to save.

verse.text: 'In your anger do not sin': Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry.

blocks.text: Notice Paul does not say 'do not be angry.' Anger is real and sometimes right. He says: in your anger, do not sin — and gives the married couple's rule: do not let the sun set on your anger. Unresolved anger does not go to sleep; it compounds. The practice is not denial but resolution before the day closes — a peace made, an apology given, a prayer said together. The verse is called 'the no-sundown rule,' and it has kept more marriages than any counseling room.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Commit to the no-sundown rule with your spouse
If you're angry now, name it and start the repair
Don't let the sun set on a word unsaid in kindness

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach us to fight within the day
Let no anger set with us

verse.text: My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry.

blocks.text: James hands the slowest art of conflict to the fastest speaker: quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger. In a fight, most of us reverse all three — slow to hear, fast to reply, fast to flare. The cure for unfair fighting is speed control: listen until the other is actually empty, not until you can interrupt. The three speeds are a sequence; if you get the first one right, the other two mostly fix themselves.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Listen to your spouse until they say 'I'm done'
Delay your reply by full minutes today
Slow the anger down by slowing the tongue down

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make me quick to hear and slow to speak
Slow my anger to the speed of love

verse.text: Where there is strife, there is pride, but wisdom is found in those who take advice.

blocks.text: The proverb diagnoses most marital fights before they even start: where there is strife, there is pride. Most arguments are not really about the dishes or the plans — they are about who has to give ground. Two pride-walls can't yield, so every small collision becomes a stalemate. Wisdom, the proverb says, is found among those who can take advice — who can receive 'maybe you're wrong' from the person they married. Drop the pride in the fight, and the fight itself usually drops.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Find the pride under today's dispute
Let that one thing go — see what happens
Receive one correction from your spouse graciously

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Plow the pride out of our fights
Make me willing to be advised by my spouse

verse.text: Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.

blocks.text: The verse imagines the inevitable: a grievance between two one-flesh people. They will rub each other raw; it comes with the closeness. And the instruction is not 'don't have grievances' — it is forgive, as the Lord forgave you. That last clause is the measuring stick and the power source: the marriage is held together by people who have already been forgiven a debt infinitely beyond what the other married person owes them. Forgive one another the way you've been forgiven.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name today's grievance to God before you name it to your spouse
Forgive it 'as the Lord forgave you' — release it
Ask if you've been holding last year's grievance too

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Forgive me, so I can forgive
Let our grievances die before they own us

verse.text: 'In your anger do not sin.'

blocks.text: Quiz day on fighting fair. One rule to own: anger may arrive, but sin must not follow. Check what you remember, then go and disagree like a Christian.

blocks.question: What is the Ephesians 4:26 rule about anger in marriage?
options: Never be angry at each other
Don't let the sun go down on your anger
Walk away until you're calm for weeks
Fight only on weekends
blocks.explain: 'In your anger do not sin: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry.' Anger is allowed; unfinished anger is not.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep our fights from sinning
Teach us to resolve before the day closes

verse.text: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the blessed title is given to the peacemaker. Not the peace-keeper (who buries everything), the peace-MAKER (who builds reconciliation). In a marriage, peacemaking is the dangerous, loving work: initiating the hard conversation, making the first move, offering the apology first. It takes more courage than the fight. Rest today in the family resemblance: when you make peace, you look like your Father.

blocks.prompt: Where is your marriage needing a peacemaker to initiate — and what would it cost you to go first?
blocks.placeholder: The peace I can make today is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make me a peacemaker in my own home
Give me the courage to go first

verse.text: But now you must also rid yourselves of all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips.

blocks.text: The week ends with a clearing of the site: rid yourselves of anger, rage, malice, slander, filthy language. These are the fight-words that must be evicted from a Christian marriage. 'Filthy language' — the profanity hurled at its own flesh — has no place between one-flesh people; calling the one flesh ugly names is cursing your own body. This week's harvest is the discipline of the emptied mouth: anger addressed, pride admitted, ridding continued daily.

blocks.prompt: Which of Paul's eviction list (anger, rage, malice, slander, filthy language) has been squatter in your conversations — and where does it keep entering from?
blocks.placeholder: The squatter I need to evict is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Evict the words that wound our flesh
Empty my mouth and refill it with grace

intro.text: Week three was about fighting fair; week four is about what happens after the damage — because even fair-fighting couples wound each other. This week is the mending: reconciliation, confession, covering love, gentle restoration, and the years the locusts ate, returned.

verse.text: All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.

blocks.text: God's first gift to marriages is the one we usually use last: reconciliation. He reconciled us to Himself — that is the fact — and then 'gave us' the ministry of reconciliation: the daily work of bringing His children back to each other. You are not inventing repair; you are administering a ministry God already funds. When your marriage needs mending, you are not starting from zero; you are working from a completed reconciliation toward the one still pending.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: See this week's healing as God's ministry to your marriage
Make the first reconciling move in a small breach today
Ask: 'who is God sending me to be reconciled with?'

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Fund our mending with Your reconciliation
Make us ministers of reconciliation first

verse.text: Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed.

blocks.text: The deepest breaches in marriages are the hidden ones — the offense carried unconfessed. James gives the healing order: confess to each other, then pray for each other, so that you may be healed. The husband who can say 'I was wrong, please forgive me' and the wife who can hear it without ammunition — that house is structurally sound. A confessed sin loses its power; a hidden one corrodes the foundation. Start small, and let the confession habit rebuild trust.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Confess one real thing, specifically, to your spouse
Hear theirs without retaliating or re-litigating
Close with prayer together over the mended spot

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give me the courage of honest confession
Heal what is healed by the telling

verse.text: Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins.

blocks.text: The breach can be so wide that only love can pour over it. 'Love covers' is not hiding or pretending — it is the covering that comes after confession: the offense is real, acknowledged, forgiven, and then covered rather than rehearsed forever. Deep love refuses to keep a running tally, refusing to drag last year's failure into this week's argument. Above all, love each other deeply — the 'above all' is the priority: when love runs this deep in the house, the covers are long enough for every breach.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Drop one replayed offense from the record
Give your spouse the covering you'd want given you
Let 'deeply' describe today's love, not 'carefully'

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make my love deep enough to cover
Teach us to be covered, not exposed

verse.text: Brothers and sisters, if someone is caught in a sin, you who live by the Spirit should restore that person gently. But watch yourselves, or you also may be tempted.

blocks.text: The heaviest breach is the serious fall — infidelity, addiction, betrayal. James' and Paul's word for the response is the same: restore that person gently, and watch yourself. Restoration is not cheap grace; it is the long, Spirit-led work of rebuilding trust — and the 'gently' protects both parties: the one restored and the one restoring. A marriage that has walked through a deep breach knows this verse by heart. Some breach, too, is no longer mending in this season; proceed honestly before God.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: If you've been the wounded one: check your gentleness
If you've been the wounding one: accept the honest road
Name one wise helper (council, pastor) you could involve

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Restore us gently by Your Spirit
Bound the deep waters You Yourself must mend

verse.text: Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed.

blocks.text: Quiz day on repair. One promise to hold: the breach is not the end of the story — His ministry is reconciliation. Check what you remember, then mend the nearest crack today.

blocks.question: What order does James 5:16 give for healing between people?
options: Wait until the offense fades
Confess to each other, then pray for each other
Forget it ever happened
Punish and move on
blocks.explain: 'Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed.' Honest words, then prayer — that is the mending order.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Mend the breach between us
Let our confession open the road to healing

verse.text: I will repay you for the years the locusts have eaten.

blocks.text: Rest day — and this is the most beautiful repair promise in Scripture: I will repay you for the years the locusts have eaten. God speaks to a devastated harvest about restoration of lost time. Couples carry eaten years — a season of distrust, of distance, of grief. And God says He is in the repayment business: not 'you'll just have to accept the lost years' but 'I will repay you for them.' Rest today in the certainty that the mender of marriages redeems time itself. Your best years are still on His ledger.

blocks.prompt: What 'eaten years' is God able to repay in your marriage? Let the promise off the hook — He mends time, not just quarrels.
blocks.placeholder: The years I'm handing Him to repay...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Repay us for the eaten years
Let restoration heal time, not just quarrels

verse.text: I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.

blocks.text: The week closes with the deepest repair of all — heart surgery. Marriages stone over: after enough wounds, a heart hardens to protect itself, and two stone hearts can't touch. God's promise is that He removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh — soft, alive, able to be hurt again, and therefore able to love again. That is the only repair that actually holds. Let week four end where all repair ends: not in managing hardened hearts, but in asking the Heart-Giver for a heart of flesh.

blocks.prompt: Where in your marriage has a heart of stone grown — and would you let God trade it for a heart of flesh this week?
blocks.placeholder: The stony place I'm surrendering is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Remove our hearts of stone
Put a living heart of flesh in us

intro.text: Money and direction are where marriages either pull together or pull apart. This week is about the two of you walking in the same direction — agreed plans, shared priorities, one purse, and the God who is the real security behind every figure on the budget.

verse.text: Do two walk together unless they have agreed to do so?

blocks.text: The prophet's question is a marriage audit: do two walk together unless they have agreed to do so? Couples drift apart not in one dramatic step but in a thousand unagreed steps — the dream not shared, the budget line not discussed, the saving plan one person knows and the other doesn't. Walking together is agreement made and kept. This week, pick the vision: where are the two of you walking? If you can't say the same sentence, that's your first project — agree, then walk.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Ask: 'where are WE walking?' — write both answers
Find the one disagreement under the drift
Agree on one direction today, no matter how small

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Unite our steps — let us walk to the same place
Show us where You are walking us

verse.text: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

blocks.text: Jesus states the law of the heart: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. It works backwards, too — put your treasure somewhere and the heart follows. That is why a couple's purse is spiritual: whatever the two of you pour money into, your hearts move there. The marriage that treasures generosity, mission, the children's faith and a shared future is a marriage whose hearts converge. Check the purse today, because it is telling you where your hearts already are.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Look at last month's spending as a heart-map with your spouse
Name one thing your purse 'treasures' that surprises you
Decide one shared treasure to invest in this month

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Show us where our treasure has taken our hearts
Let our purse follow our shared faith

verse.text: Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

blocks.text: Giving is the budget line a couple must agree on, and the verse sets the how: decided in your heart, not reluctantly, not under compulsion. Worth noting — 'each of you' — the giving is between you and God, and in marriage it must also be between the two of you: a generosity you decide together, cheerfully. The couple that can give together rarely has a purse war, because generosity is the cure for the fear money runs on. Decide what you give as one, and let cheerful be the flavor.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Discuss giving openly — not forced, decided together
Pick a cheerfulness you can both sign
Give something this week as a deliberate act, lovingly

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make us generous and cheerful in our giving
Free our purse from fear

verse.text: But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it.

blocks.text: Money wars are usually status wars — the comparison that makes a perfectly adequate house feel insufficient. Paul's arithmetic: godliness + contentment = great gain. We came in with nothing, we leave with nothing — so the middle has to be founded on something other than acquisition. The couple that has enough and knows it is richer than the couple that has more and doesn't. Contentment is not the absence of ambition; it is the presence of gratitude for what the Lord has given the two of you today.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name three 'enoughs' you already have, as a couple
Identify one comparison-driven desire — and let it go
Choose gratitude over the next acquisition

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach us godliness with contentment
Free our marriage from the comparison trap

verse.text: Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the purse. One truth to own as a couple: money is a heart-map, not just a math problem. Check what you remember, then align the two of you.

blocks.question: What does Matthew 6:21 say about treasure and the heart?
options: The heart controls the treasure
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also
Treasure has no effect on the heart
Only the wealthy have heart
blocks.explain: 'Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.' The purse reveals and routes the heart — especially in marriage.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let our one purse hold one heart
Center our treasure in You

verse.text: The blessing of the Lord brings wealth, and he adds no trouble with it.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the proverb makes a distinction worth resting on: the wealth the Lord brings has no trouble attached. He never badgers, never panics, never curses the gift He's already given. Rest is possible even in an ordinary budget because the provision, whatever its size, comes from a God who doesn't add anxiety to His gifts. Let the two of you stop straining at the purse tonight. He adds no trouble with the blessing He gives.

blocks.prompt: Where is your marriage treating the provision as 'trouble attached' — and can you rest in who gave it, above how big it is?
blocks.placeholder: The provision I can stop resenting...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let Your blessing come without our anxiety
Teach us to receive provision without trouble

verse.text: Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.

blocks.text: The week closes with the wisdom God built into the union: the two of you are each other's first counsel. Plans fail when only one person carries them (or when both rush); they succeed 'with many advisers' — and the richest counsel pool is your own pierced-together wisdom, plus the wise people God puts around you. Before the big moves, the purse and the vision, the habit of a praying couple taking counsel together, and with the church, is the difference between a plan that stands and one that quietly fails.

blocks.prompt: Which decision are you carrying alone that should be carried by the two of you — or by the church around you? Who is your 'many advisers'?

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give us the wisdom of shared counsel
Surround our plans with wise voices

intro.text: A house gets built in minutes, not seasons — the unhurried minutes a couple actually shares. This week is about the sacred and the ordinary both: the sabbath you protect together, the still mornings, and the two-or-three gathered in His name.

verse.text: He says, 'Be still, and know that I am God.'

blocks.text: The command that sounds like the least productive thing you could do is actually the most: be still, and know. Knowing God is not a lecture you attend; it is a stillness you practice. For a couple, stillness is counter-cultural — the calendar stuffed, the screens humming, the demands queued. Five still minutes, together or beside each other, where I AM GOD actually gets a hearing — that is sacred time being dug into the daily. Try it tonight: flat-out still, with the noise off.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Take five truly still minutes — no screen, no talk
Use them to know God, not to plan tomorrow
Invite your spouse to be still beside you tonight

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach our house the art of being still
Let us know You, not just know about You

verse.text: Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy.

blocks.text: The fourth commandment is the one couples break first and most: no day stop. 'Remember' — because everything in a busy house conspires to forget it. The sabbath is God's gift of the stop: one day a week where work has no permission to run the house, where rest is not a luxury but obedience. A marriage needs the shared stop desperately — it is the weekly proof that life is more than output. Protect one day, together, as the day the Lord gets dressed in. Remember the sabbath.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Look at your week: where is the stop?
Reserve the sabbath day now, before the week fills
Plan one rest thing the two of you share in it

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Grant us the seventh day as a gift
Let rest become our obedience, not our indulgence

verse.text: Let the morning bring me word of your unfailing love, for I have put my trust in you. Show me the way I should go, for to you I entrust my life.

blocks.text: David starts the day anchored: let the morning bring me word of your unfailing love. Not the headlines, not the first work message — the first word is love from God. A couple's house is built on that order: morning before the noise, God's word before the world's. Whether you pray separately before the kids wake or the two of you turn one verse over with the first coffee, the 'morning word' sets the whole day's frame. Let the morning, not the evening, have the first say.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Put God before the noise tomorrow morning
Read one verse before the first message
Tell your spouse the morning word you received

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let morning bring us word of Your love
Show us the way before the day takes us

verse.text: For where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them.

blocks.text: The smallest church on earth is an eavesdropping-sized one: where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them. That is a verse about your living room. The two of you praying together — over dinner, before bed, around a need — are literally a gathering with Jesus present. It does not need to be long or eloquent; it needs to be two. The couple that prays together has God not as an idea but as a guest, every day, in the place where they live. Gather. He is there.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Pray together — out loud, even once, today
Don't edit it; Jesus is here, He knows the mess
Make one recurring time for the two-of-you gathering

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Meet us in our living-room gathering
Let our two form Your presence in this house

verse.text: Where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them.

blocks.text: Quiz day on sacred time. One practice to own together: two gathered in His name is a church with Jesus present. Check what you remember, then go be the two.

blocks.question: What does Jesus promise in Matthew 18:20 about two or three gathered in His name?
options: They must be many
He is with them
They should gather in temples
Only elders count
blocks.explain: 'Where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them.' The couple's prayer is a gathered church with Jesus present.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep meeting us in the two-of-us
Bless the small gatherings in our house

verse.text: The Lord is my shepherd, I lack nothing.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the Shepherd's own economy: I lack nothing. Not 'I have everything' but 'I lack nothing' — the shepherd's provision matches every actual need, and rest is where the lack-less life is proved. God leads beside still waters; He makes the lying down happen in green grass. The couple that can rest says with David: whatever the sabbath looks like — genuinely taken — the shepherd has us covered. Tonight, lack nothing. Lie down in that green grass.

blocks.prompt: What would a sabbath 'lacking nothing' look like for the two of you this month? Let the shepherd plan it — and take it.
blocks.placeholder: Our green-grass sabbath would look like...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Lead us beside the still waters
Let us lack nothing as a couple

verse.text: Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful.

blocks.text: The week ends with the word that turns minutes into a life: devote. Not 'fit in some prayer' — devote yourselves, the way a couple devotes itself: wholeheartedly, more than to the screens and the striving. Two adverbs define it: watchful (paying attention, ready) and thankful (aware of what's already given). Devoted prayer is the married habit that outlasts seasons, the well everything else drinks from. Week six closes and the rhythm is set: still, sabbath, morning, together — now devoted.

blocks.prompt: What could you give up as a couple to 'devote' that time to prayer? Name the hour — and guard it like the sacred thing it is.
blocks.placeholder: The time we can devote is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Devote us to prayer — watchful, thankful
Let our marriage be rooted in the devoted hour

weeks.title: Week 7 — Faith on the same floor

intro.text: The couple's spiritual life is built on two partners standing on the same floor — not one dragging or one checking out. This week is about the way Scripture appoints the two of you: self-giving love, mutual submission, respect, and the reverence that keeps even your prayers from being hindered.

verse.text: Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.

blocks.text: The husband's standard is not 'be the leader' abstractly; it is specific and costly: love as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. That is a love measured by giving — not being right, not being served. If you're a husband, this verse sets your floor: sacrificial, washing, staying-loyal love, the kind that makes a wife feel safe rather than supervised. The word 'gave himself up' is the definition. Everything else about good husbanding is commentary.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Do one thing today that costs you, for your wife
Lead by service, not by lecture
Ask her: 'what would make you feel loved this week?'

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach me to give myself up gladly
Let my love make her safe, not small

verse.text: Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.

blocks.text: Before Paul lays out any roles, the whole paragraph begins with the two-way command: submit to one another, out of reverence for Christ. Whatever a couple decides about roles, the baseline is mutual: each one yields to the other, not out of defeat, but out of reverence for Christ. A marriage where both spouses bend toward the other is nearly unbreakable; one where neither bends stiffens and cracks. This week, bend first. Reverence sets the posture for every other duty in the house.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Choose to yield first in the next small standoff
Bend out of reverence, not out of defeat
Notice how mutual yielding changes the room

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make us quick to submit to each other
Let reverence lower us before each other

verse.text: He who finds a wife finds what is good and receives favor from the Lord.

blocks.text: The proverb refuses to let anyone treat marriage as a burden or a compromise: he who finds a wife finds what is good, and receives favor from the Lord. The marriage itself is the favor received — not the ring, the day or the status, but the person. Whatever the two of you are walking through, this is the frame: your spouse is a benefit God gave, a piece of His favor you keep. Speak of each other that way — as the favor, not the friction. It changes how a house feels.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Tell your spouse (and others): you are my favor, not my friction
Name one trait of theirs that is 'what is good'
Receive your spouse as a gift again today

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Thank You for the good You gave me in my spouse
Let me speak of them as the favor they are

days.title: That your prayers not be hindered

verse.text: Husbands, in the same way be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers.

blocks.text: Peter attaches the most startling consequence in Scripture to how a husband treats his wife: so that nothing will hinder your prayers. Unkindness, disrespect, harshness at home doesn't only hurt the marriage — it puts a brake on the couple's spiritual life. The list of right treatment is ordinary and powerful: considerate, respectful, remembering she is a fellow-heir of grace. Faith runs on the same floor when the ground floor is respect. Check your conduct at home today — and watch your prayers flow again.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Match your home conduct to your Sunday faith
Be considerate and respectful in the next exchange
Check: is anything in my conduct hindering our prayers?

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let nothing I do hinder our prayers
Make me their considerate, respectful partner

verse.text: Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.

blocks.text: Quiz day on faith on the same floor. One posture to own as a couple: mutual yielding out of reverence is the foundation. Check what you remember, then go stand on it.

blocks.question: What is the base command before any roles in Ephesians 5:21?
options: The husband always leads
Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ
The wife always yields
Only in church
blocks.explain: 'Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.' Paul's baseline for the couple's whole life is mutual — each bending toward the other.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Set us on the same floor of mutual love
Let our reverence shape our roles

days.title: Rejoice in the wife of your youth

verse.text: May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth.

blocks.text: Rest day — and it opens with a celebration command: may you rejoice in the wife of your youth. In its older language, the Proverb is a joyful defense of married delight — a couple isn't meant to merely tolerate or manage each other; they are meant to rejoice in each other. Rest today means the two of you being glad of each other on purpose: the joke, the shared memory, the ordinary fun, the friendship under the roles. Take time today to enjoy the person God gave you.

blocks.prompt: When did you last genuinely rejoice in your spouse — not love them dutifully, but delight in them? Plan one joyful thing together today.
blocks.placeholder: I will rejoice in them by...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Restore the delight in our marriage
Let me rejoice in the one You gave me

verse.text: Charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting; but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised.

blocks.text: The week ends with the most important price tag in Scripture: charm is deceptive, beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised. The verse is a couple's whole theology of value — what endures is not the externals the culture auctions but the character that fears God. That is true of husband and wife alike. Praise what lasts in each other; build your house on what won't fade. Faith on the same floor is really this: two people praising the everlasting in each other.

blocks.prompt: What do you praise first in your spouse — the passing or the everlasting? Name the godly thing you most thank God for in them, and say it to them.
blocks.placeholder: The everlasting I praise in them...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach us to prize what lasts
Let us praise the godliness in each other

intro.text: Every marriage is built on a departure: leave father and mother, cleave to spouse. This week is the delicate wisdom of honoring the families you came from while building the household you now are — boundaries that protect the union without betraying the love.

verse.text: '…and the two will become one flesh.' So they are no longer two, but one flesh.

blocks.text: Jesus' arithmetic applies at the boundary where it's hardest: between the spouse and the family of origin. 'No longer two' includes the two sets of parents — you have left them and become one. The leaving is a God-given fact, not a rebellion: the union outranks every previous loyalty. When a mother's expectations, a father's opinions, a sibling's drama press on the marriage, the one-flesh couple has a shield the Bible itself forged: we are no longer two. Protect the union that Scripture places first.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Stand with your spouse first, publicly, in the next overflow
Say 'we' before you say 'my family' in a hard call
Thank the parents you've honored while leaving

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Guard our oneness against divided loyalties
Give us wisdom to honor and still cleave

verse.text: Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the Lord your God is giving you.

blocks.text: Leaving is not dishonoring. The same Bible that joins the couple commands the honoring of parents — with a promise attached. The wisdom of week eight is holding both: the marriage is first, and the parents are honored. Honoring is not obeying everything or absorbing every opinion; it is respect that costs — care, gratitude, elder-honoring speech even when limits are held. A couple that tells their parents 'we love you, and we are one' keeps both the command and the covenant.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Do one concrete honoring thing for your parents this week
Speak of them with respect, even where you hold a boundary
Tell your spouse how you'll honor while cleaving

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach us to honor without betraying
Bless the parents we are learning to leave well

verse.text: The wise woman builds her house, but with her own hands the foolish one tears hers down.

blocks.text: The proverb assigns the building to a wisdom anyone can claim: the wise woman builds her house; the foolish one tears it down with her own hands. 'With her own hands' — the tearing is rarely dramatic; it is the running commentary, the comparison with other households, the unchecked words. The building, too, is ordinary: the tone, the atmosphere, the little traditions. Week eight widens this to the whole couple: your house is being built or torn down every day, usually by your own hands. Choose which.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Catch one 'tearing' habit this week — word, tone, comparison
Do one hands-on 'building' thing for your house
Decide today's atmosphere: build or tear?

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make our household builders, not tearers
Let our own hands do the building

verse.text: Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Unless the Lord watches over the city, the guards stand watch in vain.

blocks.text: The psalm cuts every building strategy down to size: unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. It is not a rebuke of labor — the verse assumes builders are building; it is a rebuke of self-reliance. The couple that builds by effort alone, however brilliant, labors in vain; the couple that builds with the Lord in the frame — whose plans, budgets, and parenting are offered to Him — builds a house that stands. Put the Builder in the building. Invite Him into the work before the work.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Offer today's building plan to the Lord first
Do the honest labor — and hand the outcome to Him
Build the house as if He is the General Contractor

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be the Builder of this house
Let our labor not be in vain

verse.text: So they are no longer two, but one flesh.

blocks.text: Quiz day on leave and cleave. One line to hold, kindly: no longer two, but one. Check what you remember, then guard the first-floor boundary without a fuss.

blocks.question: What is the clear line of Mark 10:8 for a married couple?
options: Marriage is a suggestion
They are no longer two, but one flesh
Parents decide for couples
Each keeps their own family first
blocks.explain: Jesus confirms Genesis: 'the two will become one flesh… no longer two, but one.' The union outranks previous loyalties — while parents are honored.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Help us hold the boundary with grace
Let our oneness be clear, kind and firm

days.title: A fruitful vine within your house

verse.text: Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the psalm paints the finished picture of the house the couple has been building: a fruitful vine within your house, olive shoots around your table. Not a status, not a number — a fruitful home. Rest is possible because the fruitfulness is described as a within: within YOUR house, around YOUR table. The two of you chose and built this place; God blesses it. Let the picture settle tonight: your own vine, your own shoots, the Lord's own blessing on it. That is enough to rest in.

blocks.prompt: What does 'fruitfulness within your own house' look like for the two of you right now — apart from anyone else's home?

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make our house fruitful within its own walls
Bless the shoots gathered around our table

verse.text: Yes, this will be the blessing for the man who fears the Lord.

blocks.text: The week closes with the psalmist's signature: this will be the blessing for the one who fears the Lord. The whole picture — fruitful spouse, children around the table, blessing from Zion, the good of Jerusalem — is God's yes to a household that lives before Him. Week eight ends where the building began: not in juggling families, but in fearing God, which makes the leaves, the cleaving, the honoring and the boundary all hold. The blessing is attached to the Lord, and your house is in His line.

blocks.prompt: In what one area of 'family politics' can the two of you fear the Lord this week instead of fearing to disappoint people?
blocks.placeholder: Where we will fear the Lord...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let the fear of the Lord order our house
Pour Your blessing on the leaves and the cleaves

intro.text: For couples with children, the family is the house's main living space — and the two of you are both of its supporting walls. This week is about raising the children as one: the mandate, the impressing-on, the discipline, and the love the children will finally inherit from watching the two of you love each other.

verse.text: Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him.

blocks.text: The psalm names the children before the strategy: heritage and reward from the Lord. Not burdens to manage, not projects to perfect — a heritage, something He entrusts to you. Parents who read their children as a trust from the Lord parent differently: less grasping (the child is His) and more generous (the child is a gift to steward, not own). Today, before one parenting decision, stand on the identity: your children are the Lord's heritage, handed into your two sets of hands together.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Say, with your spouse: 'our children are His heritage'
Treat one child as a trust, not a task, today
Thank God for each child by name

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Help us steward Your heritage
Let us raise them as Yours, not ours alone

verse.text: These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.

blocks.text: The discipleship curriculum has a location, and it isn't the classroom — it's the daily: sitting at home, walking, lying down, getting up. Notice the order: the commands must first be on YOUR hearts before you impress them on the children. Children catch what's on the parents' hearts more than what's on the parents' lips. The two of you teaching as one — over meals, on the school run, by bedtime — is the most powerful Bible class ever scheduled.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Keep the Word on your own heart before you teach it
Talk one truth naturally at a meal or in the car
Align your two voices about one value this week

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Put Your words on our hearts first
Help us impress them in the ordinary hours

verse.text: Whoever spares the rod hates their children, but the one who loves their children is careful to discipline them.

blocks.text: The hardest verse of parenting is also the kindest: discipline is defined as an act of love, and its absence is defined as hate. The 'rod' here is the whole authority of correction — not cruelty, not venting; 'careful' discipline, the steady, loving correction that is neither a shrug nor a storm. For a couple, discipline in unison means one standard the children can't play off: two parents who back each other, correct privately, and never make the child feel like a battlefield. Careful. Loving. Together.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Agree on this week's one standard, as a couple
Correct carefully — calm, fair, consistent
Never make your child overhead a parenting disagreement

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give us the wisdom of careful discipline
Let our unity be our children's safety

verse.text: Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

blocks.text: Paul's word to parents starts on the defensive side: do not exasperate — don't provoke, don't over-command, don't set a standard of perfection the child can never reach, don't make love conditional. The 'instead' is training and instruction in the Lord. The two of you parent in unison best when you're clear which direction is training and which is vexation. Watch today's pace: is the child being trained toward the Lord, or merely worn down by your noise? Kids rarely forget the tone.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Notice one exasperating pattern to retire
Train patiently toward one virtue today
Keep love unconditional above performance

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep our words from exasperating
Let our training aim them at You

verse.text: Children are a heritage from the Lord.

blocks.text: Quiz day on parenting in unison. One frame to hold: the children are His heritage, and the two of you are His stewards. Check what you remember, then go parent as one.

blocks.question: What are children called in Psalm 127:3?
options: A burden to manage
A heritage and reward from the Lord
A project to perfect
An accident of fate
blocks.explain: 'Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him.' Stewardship, not ownership.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Help us raise Your heritage as one
Keep us unified for the children's sake

verse.text: Children's children are a crown to the aged, and parents are the pride of their children.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the proverb gives the long view: grandchildren a crown, parents the pride of their children. Parenting in unison is a seed-planting sureness that the harvest is decades away. The crown is worn by the aged — meaning the work you're doing now pays the future its interest. Rest, because the proverb lets you release the need to see it all now. Children grow up; children have children; steady parents become the pride of the ones they trained. The unison you build today is a crown decades from now.

blocks.prompt: What one daily consistency, kept up for a decade, would your future self thank you for? Rest in the long-view proverb tonight.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let the long view settle our impatience
Make our consistency their crown

verse.text: A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another.

blocks.text: The week closes on the secret of the whole house: children inherit their parents' love for each other more than anything they're told. 'As I have loved you' — Jesus sets the pattern, and the children are watching it live in the kitchen every night. The kindest thing you ever do for your children is incarnate — love their other parent visibly, warmly, and them second; they flourish in that climate. Week nine's final stone: love each other as Christ loved, and the children will know the love of God by its human address.

blocks.prompt: What is the most loving thing your children have ever witnessed between the two of you? How can that live more in this season?
blocks.placeholder: The love our children have seen...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let our children inherit our love for each other
Model to them the love of Christ

intro.text: A couple is built to give, not just to protect. This week is about the joy of serving side by side — each other, the household, the church, and the world — because the strongest marriages are pointers, aimed outward, and love is the family business.

verse.text: You, my brothers and sisters, were called to be free. But do not use your freedom to indulge the flesh; rather, serve one another humbly in love.

blocks.text: Freedom is not the point of freedom — service is. Paul warns a newly-free people: don't use the liberty to indulge the flesh; use it to serve one another humbly in love. In a marriage, 'serve one another' is the operating system: not 'who owes who' but 'how can I serve you today, humbly, in love.' A couple out-servicing each other stops keeping score — and the scorekeeping is what rots households. Serve first. Watch the marriage follow.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Ask your spouse: 'how can I serve you today?' — then do it
Serve humbly: no invoice, no tally
Choose your spouse's need over your convenience once

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make us servants of each other first
Free us from the scorekeeping

days.title: Not to be served, but to serve

verse.text: just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

blocks.text: Jesus gives the couple's mission statement in one sentence: the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve. The divine whole life is defined by serving — and He says 'just as,' making it the pattern for every follower and every family. The house that runs on 'who serves next' instead of 'who deserves what' is the house that looks like Jesus. When the argument comes, the first question isn't 'who's right?' — it's 'who will serve?' Serve, because He did, ransom for many, ransom included your marriage.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Do one unnoticed service today
Serve without being asked or praised
Let 'not to be served' reset your next argument

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Conform our serving to Yours
Let us prefer the towel to the throne

verse.text: Now that I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another's feet.

blocks.text: Jesus stoops to the dirtiest job — the guest-cleanup of dusty feet — and says: you also should wash one another's feet. The unforgettable part is who did it: the Lord and Teacher. No rank exempts a marriage from the towel and basin. In a household, 'feet-washing' is the unglamorous load — the dishes again, the school notes, the night wake-up, the laundry cycle. A couple that happily takes the towel is a couple that stays clean of pride. Watch who stoops in your house this week — and trade turns.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Do the foot-washing job nobody thanked you for
Notice your spouse's towel — and lift yours
Serve the menial service Jesus stooped to

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Stoop with me into the small services
Let me serve without the spotlight

verse.text: Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves, not looking to your own interests but each of you to the interests of the others.

blocks.text: Paul presses the married couple's hardest discipline: in humility value others above yourselves, look to the interests of others. Not 'also' or 'sometimes' — 'above,' and 'not to your own but to theirs.' This is the anti-ambition of the house: the argument where neither spouse is looking at the other's interest is the argument nobody wins. A couple who each champion the other's interests has two champions in every room. That is the strongest team in the world, and it lives at your house.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: In the next exchange, look to your spouse's interest first
Champion their ambition out loud today
Do nothing out of selfish ambition today

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give us eyes for each other's interests
Kill the selfish ambition in our house

verse.text: Serve one another humbly in love.

blocks.text: Quiz day on service. One posture to own as a couple: serving each other is the house's operating system, and the towel beats the throne. Check what you remember, then go serve.

blocks.question: According to Galatians 5:13, what were we called to be free to do?
options: Whatever we want
Serve one another humbly in love
Pursue personal gain
Avoid one another
blocks.explain: 'You… were called to be free. But do not use your freedom… rather, serve one another humbly in love.' Freedom's purpose is service.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let our freedom be for serving
Make service the family business

days.title: Work at it with all your heart

verse.text: Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the rest arrives at the strangest rest-verse in the Bible: work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord. The rest is in the audience change: the drudgery of the household isn't done for human masters — the demanding boss, the ungrateful family member, the thankless pile — but for the Lord, who sees every dish and every diaper. That single shift settles the soul's wind. Work at it all-heartedly because you're serving Him, and suddenly rest isn't escaping the load; rest is knowing Whose load it is.

blocks.prompt: Which household service have you been doing 'for human masters'? Re-frame it tonight as work for the Lord — and feel the rest land.
blocks.placeholder: The service I will offer to the Lord...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let our labor be offered to You
Settle our hearts in whose service we work

verse.text: Give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over, will be poured into your lap.

blocks.text: The week ends at the only economy that always pays: give, and it will be given to you — a good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over. The couple whose house is a giving-house — serving each other, their church, their neighbors, the world — taps a supply that out-measures any budget. The 'running over' is God's own arithmetic for a generous household. Give the two of you away this season: your hours, your home, your hands. The lap that receives is wider than the giving arms. Try the running-over math.

blocks.prompt: What could your couple offer that no one else can — hospitality, skills, a listening home? Give one real thing this week, and watch the measure.
blocks.placeholder: The one gift we can give is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make us a generous, giving house
Let Your good measure run over for others

intro.text: The house's deepest choice is not its paint or even its repairs — it is its foundation. This week is about the rock under everything: hearing Jesus' words and putting them into practice, the one Foundation laid, and the storm that proves which material you used.

verse.text: Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.

blocks.text: The whole Sermon on the Mount funnels into one contrast — two builders, one rock, one sand — and the difference between them is not IQ or income. It is exactly this: hears these words and puts them into practice. Both heard; only one practiced. A marriage built on the rock is built out of practiced obedience — forgiveness practiced, words guarded, sabbath kept, service done — not just Bible talk. The wise couple isn't the theologian couple; it's the doing couple. Practice the words, and your house's address is the rock.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Pick one of His words to actually practice today
Do it with your spouse watching — practice is public
Check: are we hearing people or doing people?

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make us doers, not just hearers
Let our practices build on the Rock

verse.text: The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because it had its foundation on the rock.

blocks.text: Here is what the sermon never hides: the storm comes for BOTH houses. The wise man's house gets rained on exactly as hard as the fool's. The foundation is not the guarantee of no storm; it is the guarantee of standing IN the storm. Every marriage will be rained on — a lost job, a sick child, a hard financial season, a dark night of the soul. The question the sermon forces today is not 'will storms come' but 'when the storm beats against US, what is our house standing on?'

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name the storm you're in or the one brewing
Ask together: what is holding our house up?
Re-anchor the foundation this week, before it's shaking

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be the Rock under our house in the storm
Let us not fall when the weather comes

days.title: By wisdom a house is built

verse.text: By wisdom a house is built, and through understanding it is established.

blocks.text: The wise-builders are wisdom-builders: by wisdom a house is built, and through understanding it is established. Wisdom is what the couple collects on purpose — from Scripture, from the church, from honest counsel, from the costly lessons of their own mistakes. Houses get built one wise choice at a time and established one understanding at a time. The couple that stops learning stops building. Ask together this week: what do we need to understand better to stand firmer? Then go get that wisdom.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name one area where your marriage needs more wisdom
Get some: a study, a book, a counselor, a question to God
Turn one mistake into established understanding

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give us the wisdom to build
Let understanding establish us

verse.text: through knowledge its rooms are filled with rare and beautiful treasures.

blocks.text: The second half of the proverb describes the furnished house: through knowledge its rooms are filled with rare and beautiful treasures. A house built in wisdom gets FURNISHED in knowledge — the rooms aren't just walls; they're stocked with treasure: shared memory, gathered truth, the wealth of a life taught and loved. A couple that reads, prays, learns, and collects good things fills their house with heritage that outlasts furniture. Establish the house, then furnish it — each year adding rare and beautiful treasures to the rooms of your shared life.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Inventory one 'room' — what treasure is in it?
Add one rare-and-beautiful thing: memory, truth, habit
Learn one new thing together this week

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Fill our house with lasting treasures
Let knowledge enrich our rooms

verse.text: Built his house on the rock.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the rock. One question every couple must answer: what is our house really standing on — His words practiced, or our own convenience? Check what you remember, then inspect the foundation.

blocks.question: According to Matthew 7:24–25, what is the difference between the wise and foolish builders?
options: The wise had no storms
The wise heard AND put His words into practice
The wise had more money
The wise avoided the rain
blocks.explain: Both heard His words and both got rained on. The wise one practiced — that practice is the foundation that stands.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Show us what our house is built on
Let practice, not talk, lay our foundation

days.title: I know whom I have believed

verse.text: …I know whom I have believed, and am convinced that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the rested foundation is personal before it is architectural: I know whom I have believed. Not 'I know what I believe' — the foundation is a person. The couple can rest because the Rock is not an idea they're maintaining; He is the living One guarding what they've entrusted to Him. The marriage, the children, the future — deposited with Him. Rest tonight in the deposit. The house stands because the Guard is alive, and the guard has the whole thing entrusted to His care until that day.

blocks.prompt: What of your marriage — the fragile, unfinished parts — can you formally entrust to the Guard today? Let the conviction, not the fear, do the speaking.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Guard what we have entrusted to You
Let us rest in whom, not what, we believe

days.title: The Lord knows those who are his

verse.text: Nevertheless, God's solid foundation stands firm, sealed with this inscription: 'The Lord knows those who are his.'

blocks.text: The week closes on the confidence that is deeper than any storm forecast: God's solid foundation stands firm, and its seal reads the Lord knows those who are his. Whatever wavers in your marriage — feelings, plans, circumstances — the foundation itself is not contingent. It stands, and its security is a knowing: God knows you, knows you are His, in a way no wind can touch. Week eleven's last stone is the best one: your marriage is built over, and knit into, a foundation that cannot shift, sealed with your name in the Knower's hand.

blocks.prompt: What would change in how you face this season's uncertainties if you believed the seal — 'the Lord knows those who are His' — was stamped over your house?
blocks.placeholder: If the seal is over us...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let our house rest on Your firm foundation
Seal us with the knowledge that we are Yours

intro.text: Marriage is not a contract with an exit clause; it is a covenant — sworn before God and the witnesses, a seal over the heart, faithfulness bound on like an oath kept even when it hurts. This week is about honoring the promise when the feelings flag and the pressure mounts.

verse.text: It is because the Lord is the witness between you and the wife of your youth. You have been unfaithful to her, though she is your partner, the wife of your marriage covenant.

blocks.text: Malachi speaks through the broken marriages of his day to name what marriage is: a covenant with a witness. 'The Lord is the witness between you and the wife of your youth.' The covenant was not made only between two people — it was made before God, with Him as witness. That is what makes it unbreakable by whim. When the feelings wobble or the culture whispers 'you've changed,' the covenant holds the line: this is not a contract to renegotiate; it is an oath with a Witness, sworn to the one you vowed before Him.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Re-remember your vows with your spouse — read or say them
Treat God as the Witness present in today's choices
Close one small leak of unfaithfulness (eyes, heart, words)

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep me faithful to my covenant
Let the Witness govern my faithfulness

verse.text: Let love and faithfulness never leave you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart.

blocks.text: The proverb dresses the covenant-keeper: let love and faithfulness never leave you — bind them around your neck, so they're seen; write them on the tablet of your heart, so they last. Love and faithfulness are a matched set: love without faithfulness fades into romance; faithfulness without love hardens into duty. Bind them on like a visible garment and they become your reputation in the house: the spouse people can count on. Tablets of the heart are what you engrave when no one is watching your choices. Engrave them today.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Let your 'yes' to your spouse be a 'yes' today
Bind faithfulness visibly — keep the small promises
Engrave the heart-tablet with love that lasts

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Bind love and faithfulness on me
Write on my heart what endures

verse.text: Place me like a seal over your heart, like a seal on your arm; for love is as strong as death.

blocks.text: The Song's covenant image is a signet seal — the personal stamp pressed into wax, making a binding mark. Place me like a seal over your heart: the beloved asks to be worn not as an accessory but as the very imprint of who you are. 'Love is as strong as death' — death ends everything else; this love shares death's authority without its bitterness. A covenant marriage wears the seal: over the heart (wanting is guarded) and on the arm (acting is faithful). Press the seal today — heart and hand — so the imprint shows in both places.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Print the seal on your heart: guard the wanting
Print it on your arm: act faithfully all day
Be the spouse whose 'for better/worse' shows in the seal

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Seal me over heart and arm
Let this love be as strong as death

verse.text: Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the adulterer and all the sexually immoral.

blocks.text: The verse states the covenant's guardrails in both directions: marriage honored by all, the bed kept pure — and the warning against adultery is real, with God named as judge. 'Honored by all' includes the couple themselves: the way you speak of your marriage, defend it, and refuse whatever cheapens it. Purity in a marriage is a project, not an accident — the eyes, the conversations, the places, the habits decided ahead. Guard the honored-to-all marriage this week: guard it publicly in what you praise, and privately in what you don't let in.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Honor your marriage in your speech today — defend it
Set one guardrail where your eyes or time wander
Praise your spouse publicly; keep your vows privately

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep our marriage honored and our bed pure
Guard the place only You see

verse.text: Place me like a seal over your heart.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the covenant. One distinction to own: marriage is a covenant with a Witness, not a contract with an exit. Check what you remember, then press the seal again.

blocks.question: What makes a biblical marriage a covenant rather than a contract?
options: Both parties signed papers
God is the witness between the two
It lasts nine years
It can be dissolved by mutual consent
blocks.explain: Malachi 2:14: 'The Lord is the witness between you and the wife of your youth.' A covenant stands before God — that's why it holds.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let us live as covenanted, not contracted
Keep the Witness at the center of our vows

verse.text: For the Lord loves the just and will not forsake his faithful ones.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the covenant-keepers get a rest-word with a promise: the Lord will not forsake his faithful ones. The faithfulness you're practicing — through the flat season, the hard year, the ordinary grind — is seen and held. God keeps covenant with covenant-keepers; His faithfulness is the deep water your smaller faithfulness floats on. Rest tonight in the One who will not forsake you. The seal you press is a small impression of the great seal He has already pressed on you — and His never lets go.

blocks.prompt: Where has your faithfulness felt unnoticed — and can you rest in the One who has promised not to forsake His faithful ones?
blocks.placeholder: I can rest my faithfulness in...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Remind me You do not forsake the faithful
Let my keeping of vows rest in Your keeping of me

days.title: An oath even when it hurts

verse.text: …who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and does not change their mind.

blocks.text: The week ends with the covenant-keeper's profile in one phrase: keeps an oath even when it hurts, and does not change their mind. That is the whole of it — the oath kept on the hard afternoons, the vow that doesn't get renegotiated in the valley. Covenant faithfulness is not the absence of pain; it is the keeping through it. Week twelve closes on the strongest foundation a couple can stand on: a promise made before God, kept when it hurts, never reconsidered. That promise, kept by both of you, is what makes the house unshakable.

blocks.prompt: When has keeping your oath 'even when it hurts' already proven its steel? And what is the next hurting thing you'll keep through anyway?

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give me the strength to keep the oath in the pain
Let me not change my mind on what I swore

weeks.title: Week 13 — A house with open doors

intro.text: The strongest house is not the shuttered fortress; it is the open house — a door the neighborhood can knock on, a table set wide, a home that makes Christ visible. This week closes the season by turning the building into a welcome.

verse.text: Share with the Lord's people who are in need. Practice hospitality.

blocks.text: The Romans 12 list of the Christian life hands the couple a regular practice: share with the Lord's people who are in need, practice hospitality. 'Practice' is the word that matters — hospitality is a skill maintained by repetition, not a talent some couples have. In the New Testament, hospitality is largely a home-based ministry: the open door, the extended table, the room for the traveler, the meal shared with the single, the widow, the stranger. The couple that practices it turns their house from a residence into a ministry. Start small — this season, one door opened is enough.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Open your door once this month — a meal, a visitor
Look around your church for 'who is in need'
Decide together: who is our first guest?

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make our house a practice of hospitality
Show us who You are sending to our door

verse.text: Do not forget to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have shown hospitality to angels without knowing it.

blocks.text: The verse attaches the loveliest suspense to the open door: show hospitality to strangers — and some who did have entertained angels without knowing it. You never know in whose face God visits. The child from the broken home who shows up for dinner, the newcomer at church nobody has over, the neighbor in a season of need — each one is the possible angel, the disguised Christ who said 'I was a stranger and you invited me in.' Love the stranger at your door, because the Open-Door God has a habit of showing up behind surprising faces.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Think of one 'stranger' your house could welcome
Welcome Christ by welcoming a stranger this month
Keep a door unlatched in your heart

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let us welcome You in the stranger
Keep our house ready for the angel who knocks

verse.text: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.

blocks.text: The Shepherd's hospitality is the pattern for the family's: you prepare a table before me. God hosts us in the presence of trouble — the table is not set after the enemies leave; it is spread right in the middle of the press. That is the model the couple's table runs on: the table where the family sits even in a hard season, the table set in the presence of anxiety and loss. And the table that receives the Shepherd's hosting becomes a table that can host others. Eat after the Shepherd, then set a table that says: God prepared one for me.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Sit at the table God set for you — family, meal, thanks
Set a table 'in the presence' — host through the hard
Let the overflowing cup become a poured-out one

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Prepare a table for us even in trouble
Let our table host what Yours has hosted

days.title: Invite the ones who can't repay

verse.text: But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed.

blocks.text: Jesus redefines the guest list: when you give a banquet, don't invite the people who can invite you back — invite the ones who can't repay. That is the open-door economics that keeps hospitality from becoming social climbing. The couple's table, aimed at the people who have nothing to offer in return, becomes a blessed table — because the blessing is attached to the un-repayable invitation. Check your guest list's direction this week: not 'who will RSVP us back' but 'who has no door of their own?'

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Invite someone who can't repay you, this month
Strip the banquet of its required returns
Bless by hosting the ones who can't host back

blocks.title: Pray it today
